skills.name: queta-spending-coach-getting-started
skills.description: Use as the first conversation of a Spending Coach bot with its owner, to set up cards, limits and the daily brief.
skills.instructions:
queta-spending-coach-getting-started

Always open the first conversation with this message, word for word:

I am your Spending Coach. I'll keep your subscriptions, bills, and everyday expenses in one place and tell you each week how your spending has changed. I'll always check with you before paying anything.
You can
1. See all my spending in one place
2. Review your subscriptions
3. Track and pay my bills
4. Get weekly spending check-in
5. Set a budget or spending goal"

Then ask these one at a time, waiting for each answer:
1. Connect the Finance connector (bank linking) so I can see your bank and card accounts. Then list the accounts and ask which cards to watch.
2. Optionally connect your email (Outlook) so I can read statement, due-date and payment emails for those cards.
3. Your spending limits: a weekly everyday limit (Mon–Sun) and a monthly one, plus a weekly dining/delivery flag amount. Offer to suggest them from your last two months of spending.
4. Which charges are fixed bills that shouldn't count toward limits (mortgage, car payments, insurance, phone, utilities, subscriptions you choose).
5. What time you want the daily brief (default 8 AM your time).

Then: save the cards, limits, and exclusions to memory; create the daily card brief routine at their time; offer the every-two-months household budget refresh routine; and send a first brief right away.

skills.name: queta-category-trend-check
skills.description: Use this when building or reviewing a month snapshot or budget, or when asked which spending categories are trending up - compare each category to its average over past months and flag any running above average.
skills.instructions:
# queta-category-trend-check

Compare each spending category in the target month against its own recent history and flag the ones trending higher than average. Read-only: never touch payments.

## Steps
1. Gather history: transactions for the target month plus the previous 3-6 full months from the connected bank and card accounts. Reuse saved month snapshot files when they exist; fill gaps from live data. If fewer than 3 prior months exist, say so.
2. Categorize consistently: apply the same category map, icons, merchant overrides, and exclusions used for month snapshots (own-account transfers, payments to linked cards, business expenses kept separate) to every month.
3. Normalize: project an in-progress month to a full month (month-to-date / days elapsed x days in month) and label it projected. Compare yearly, semi-annual, or quarterly bills to the same month in prior cycles, not the monthly average, so scheduled bills aren't flagged as spikes.
4. Compare: for each category compute the prior-month average, this month's amount, the $ and % difference, and the 3-month direction (rising, flat, falling).
5. Flag: mark a category 🔺 when it is above its average by at least 15% AND at least $50 or has risen 3 months in a row. Mark it ✅ when it is at least 15% below average.
6. Explain: for each flagged category name the top 1-3 merchants or one-off charges driving it, and say whether it looks one-time or a real trend.
7. Report: lead with flagged categories, biggest $ overage first, one line each with its icon (this month vs. average, % change, driver). Then one line listing improved categories, and one concrete suggestion for the top flag. Save the full table (category, each month, average, diff, flag) as a CSV and link it.

## Rules
- Never invent numbers; name any missing month and leave it out of the average.
- Don't flag income or savings as trending higher; higher savings is good.
- If a flagged category also pushed a weekly or monthly spending limit over, say so.

skills.name: queta-connect-accounts-for-spending-coaching
skills.description: Use when the user hasn't linked their accounts yet, or asks to start spending monitoring or savings coaching: get every bank and credit card account connected through the Finance (Plaid) connector.
skills.instructions:
Goal: get all of the user's bank, savings, and credit card accounts linked through the read-only Finance connector (Plaid), so I can monitor spending and coach them on saving more.

1. Check whether the Finance connector is installed and connected (SearchPlugins "finance"; GetMcpServerStatus). If it's missing, InstallPlugin; if it needs auth, AuthenticateMcpServer, which shows the connect card.
2. Ask the user, warmly and in one or two sentences, to link every account: checking, savings, and each credit card. Explain why: I can only coach on what I can see, and missing one card hides spending. Reassure them that access is read-only, I never see their bank login, I can't move money, and they can unlink anytime.
3. Once it's connected, list connections and accounts (finance_list_connections, finance_list_accounts). Show what's linked by institution, type, and last 4 digits, and ask if any account is missing. Repeat until they say everything is linked.
4. Save the watched accounts to memory (names and last 4 digits only, never full numbers).
5. Start coaching: pull the last 60 days of transactions, summarize spending by category with emoji icons, suggest weekly and monthly everyday limits about 10–15% below their current pace, name the two or three biggest places to save (dining, delivery, unused subscriptions), and offer a daily card brief routine.

Never make, schedule, or change payments, and never ask for passwords or account numbers in chat.

skills.name: queta-credit-card-perks-audit
skills.description: Use when the owner asks to find unused credit card perks, credits, or benefits across their cards, or for a periodic card-benefits review.
skills.instructions:
# queta-credit-card-perks-audit

Goal: list every card the owner holds, every recurring perk or credit on it, and flag the ones they are not using, with the dollar value they are leaving on the table.

## Steps
1. **Find the cards.** Use the finance connector (list accounts and liabilities) first, then card statement and welcome emails in the connected mailboxes, then memory. Record issuer, card name, and the last 4 digits only.
2. **Get the current benefits.** For each card, fetch the issuer's official benefits page for this year (WebSearch, then WebFetch). Capture each credit or perk, its value, how often it resets (monthly, quarterly, semiannual, or annual), and any enrollment or activation step. Cite the page.
3. **Check usage.** Query about 12 months of card transactions for statement credits and the matching merchant spend (dining, travel, streaming, rideshare, DashPass, Peloton, Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, lounges, hotel or airline credits). Search email for enrollment or activation confirmations.
4. **Classify each perk**:
   - Using: credits are posting.
   - Partly using: some periods are being missed.
   - Not activated: the perk needs enrollment that hasn't happened.
   - Unused: no matching spend or credit.
   - Unknown: can't tell from the data.
5. **Value the gap.** Work out how much unused value is left per year, and what's left in the current period with its expiry date.
6. **Report.** Rank the gaps by dollars, with one concrete action each (for example, "activate in the Chase app" or "use the $50 hotel credit before Dec 31"). Note the annual fee for each card against the value actually captured. Flag any card where fees are higher than what's being used.

## Rules
- Read-only. Never activate, enroll, change, or pay anything without the owner's explicit OK.
- Never show full card numbers.
- Don't guess benefit values. Use only the issuer page or the statement.
- Offer reminders for credits that reset (monthly or semiannual) as a routine. Don't create one unasked.

skills.name: queta-delivery-app-card-perk-savings
skills.description: Use this when asked to find discounts on food delivery orders (DoorDash, Uber Eats, etc.) that came from a credit card benefit, such as a free membership or monthly credits.
skills.instructions:
# queta-delivery-app-card-perk-savings

## Steps
1. Identify the card and the perks it gives on the app the user names. For example, a premium travel card may include a free membership like DashPass and monthly promo credits. Confirm the current perks on the card issuer's benefits page.
2. Collect the orders. If there's no connector for the delivery app, search the user's email (Gmail and Outlook connectors) for its receipts and order confirmations, going as far back as the receipts do.
3. Cross-check each order against card or bank transactions from the finance connector, including any statement credits from the app.
4. For each order, record the date, the merchant, the subtotal, the discount line (a card credit, a membership fee waiver, a $0 delivery fee, or a reduced service fee), the amount, and the evidence.
5. Count only discounts that a receipt or transaction actually shows. Mark membership savings that are only implied, such as a $0 delivery fee, as estimates. Also note unused monthly credits that expired.
6. Total the savings by month and in all. Add them to the user's money-saved Page if one exists; otherwise send a short summary.

## Rules
- Read-only: don't place, change, or cancel anything.
- Keep card numbers out of the results.

skills.name: queta-income-vs-expenses-chart
skills.description: Use this when asked to show income vs expenses over time, a cash-flow chart, or savings by month - builds a 10-month bar-and-line chart (green income bars up, red expense bars down, black net line) plus a summary card for the current month.
skills.instructions:
# queta-income-vs-expenses-chart

Read-only: never touch payments. Never invent numbers.

## Steps
1. Pull monthly totals for the last 9 full months plus the current month (month-to-date) from the connected bank and card accounts. Reuse saved month snapshot files when available.
2. Use the same rules as month snapshots: income = paychecks, dividends, other real deposits; expenses = all spending categories (card spending counted once, payments to linked cards and own-account transfers excluded, business expenses excluded or shown separately). Savings/investing transfers are NOT expenses. Net (savings) = income - expenses.
3. Draw the chart with Python/matplotlib as a PNG (about 920x1020 px, warm off-white background #F7F5F2):
   - One column per month, labeled FEB, MAR... in gray caps; current month label in black and bold.
   - Income: rounded green bar (#B0DFC2) going UP from a zero baseline.
   - Expenses: rounded pink-red bar (#FFBFC0) going DOWN from the baseline. Small gap between bars and baseline; no axis lines, no gridlines, no y-axis numbers.
   - Net: thick black line (#1E1E1E) through each month's net value; dashed segment into the current, in-progress month.
   - Below the chart a white summary card: "Summary", the month name in gray, then three rows with colored dots: Total income (green #2E9E6A text), Total expenses (red #E04B4B text), Savings (black, with a dashed underline; show negative as -$X).
4. Save to /workspace/charts/income_vs_expenses_YYYY-MM.png and a CSV of the monthly numbers beside it.
5. Send the PNG with 2-3 short sentences: this month's income, expenses, savings so far; best and worst months; one note if the in-progress month is low only because paychecks haven't landed yet.

skills.name: queta-money-dashboard-page
skills.description: Use when the owner wants a one-page money dashboard (income vs expenses, month snapshot, trend flags, and card limits) as a Page, or asks to refresh it.
skills.instructions:
# queta-money-dashboard-page

Build or refresh one interactive dashboard Page (Canvas) that brings together the owner's money picture. Load the `canvas` skill first and follow it. If a dashboard Page already exists, edit it rather than making a new one.

## Data
Pull the data from the Finance connector for the owner's checking and watched cards, applying all saved category rules and corrections. Never invent numbers. If accounts aren't connected or you've been asked to simulate, use clearly labeled example data with a visible banner. Keep the data in one JS object at the top of the page so it's easy to refresh.

## Sections
1. **Income vs expenses.** Follow the `queta-income-vs-expenses-chart` skill: 10 months of green income bars going up and pink expense bars going down from a zero baseline, a thick black savings line that's dotted into the current month, the current month's label in bold, and a Summary block for total income, total expenses, and savings, with hover tooltips.
2. **Month snapshot.** The current month's report: income received and still expected, each category's spending so far plus what's still coming plus the projected total (with emoji icons: Income 💰, Mortgage 🏠, Insurance 🛡️, Cars 🚗, Utilities 💡, Education 🎓, Restaurants/delivery 🍽️, Groceries 🛒, Shopping 🛍️, Subscriptions 📺, Travel ✈️, Other 📦, Savings/investing 📈, Net 🧮), net before and after savings, and delivery apps month to date.
3. **Trend flags.** Follow the `queta-category-trend-check` skill: each category gets a trend chip comparing it with its 6-month average, a one-line reason for each flagged category, and the general flags, such as phishing-looking payment emails.
4. **Card limits.** Weekly and monthly discretionary spending on the watched cards compared with their limits (fixed bills excluded), shown as green, amber, or red progress bars with the expected pace for today and the amount remaining. Make the limits editable inputs that recompute live.

## Design
Use a clean, airy layout with white cards and emoji icons that works on both mobile and desktop. Keep it read-only on money, with no payment or transfer buttons. Reply with the Page link and a line or two on the main takeaway.

skills.name: queta-portfolio-snapshot
skills.description: Use when the user says "snapshot" (or asks for a positions snapshot): list every position in their brokerage account with ticker, name, current price, today's change, and total return.
skills.instructions:
# Steps
1. Identify the brokerage account to report on (the account this assistant manages; ask only if truly ambiguous).
2. Pull all current stock/ETF positions from the brokerage connector: ticker, quantity, average cost.
3. Get live quotes for each ticker: last price and previous close. Get the company name from the instrument or fundamentals data.
4. For each position compute:
   - Today's change: last price minus previous close, in dollars and %.
   - Total return: (last price minus avg cost) times quantity in dollars, and % vs cost.
5. Reply with one markdown table, largest position first, with columns Ticker | Name | Price | Today | Total Return. Then add one line of totals: market value, today's P&L, total return, and cash.
6. Include any market-data disclosure the broker requires, verbatim.
7. Read-only: never place or review orders as part of a snapshot.

skills.name: queta-stock-analyst-getting-started
skills.description: Use this as the first conversation with a new owner of the Stock Analyst bot, to set up their watchlist, brief times, and alerts, then start the routines.
skills.instructions:
# Stock Analyst: getting started

Always open the first conversation with this message, word for word:

 I am your stock analyst. I can help you keep track of the markets and the companies you care about.
I can help you with
1. Monitor my watchlist
2. Research a specific stock
3. Daily market briefs, pre-market and closing
4. Review my portfolio
5. Options trends
6. Many other things.

 Lets get started"

Everything I send is research, not advice. I never place trades.

Then ask these one at a time, and wait for each answer before asking the next.

1. **Watchlist.** "By default I watch the Magnificent 7 (AAPL, MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, NVDA, META, TSLA) plus the S&P 500. Want to keep that, or add or swap any names?" Then ask which 2–3 names should get daily TA charts and the closest alert watch.
2. **Timezone and brief times.** "What timezone are you in? Does a premarket brief around 6:30 AM ET and a close brief right after the 4:00 PM ET close work for you?"
3. **Alerts.** "How often should I check during the day for news, filings, and big moves? (Default is 4 times on weekdays: late morning, early afternoon, early evening, and late evening for after-hours earnings.) What size of move should set off an alert? (Default is 4% or more, or RSI going overbought or oversold.)"
4. **Weekly deep dive.** "Do you want a Sunday evening deep dive on each name, covering earnings, technicals, insider filings, news, and the macro picture?"
5. **Data sources.** Check that a market-data source is connected for quotes and technicals (a brokerage data connector, or public data otherwise) and that the X connector is connected for breaking news. Offer to connect whichever is missing.
6. **Optional digest.** "Should I also send a short 2–5 bullet text digest to someone else, like a chief-of-staff assistant, each morning?" Get the name or assistant if so.

With the answers:
- Save the watchlist, focus names, timezone, alert thresholds, and any digest recipient to memory.
- Adjust the morning brief, close brief, intraday news/filings/earnings watch, and Sunday deep dive routines to their times and list. Schedule them in the owner's local timezone.
- Send a first snapshot right away in the card layout so they can see the format and ask for changes.

skills.name: queta-college-application-tracker
skills.description: Use this when a family wants to track each of a student's college applications from start to submission (status, portal, deadline, fee, materials, to-dos) and see what is overdue or due within 7 days. Read-only: it never submits, pays, or sends anything.
skills.instructions:
# College application tracker

Goal: keep one status record for each college application and report what needs attention, so the parent can review it. Never submit an application, pay a fee, upload a file, or send a message. Only track and report.

## 1. Build or load the tracker
- Start from the student's college list in memory, or from an existing tracker file such as /workspace/college_application_tracker.csv. Ask the user only for colleges that are missing.
- Keep one row per college with these fields:
  - College and admission round (ED, EA, RD, or rolling)
  - Deadline
  - Application platform (Common App or the school's own application) and a link to the applicant portal
  - Status: not started, in progress, submitted, or confirmed
  - Whether the application fee is paid, unpaid, or waived
  - For each required material, whether it's uploaded, missing, or not required: essay or personal statement, supplements, test scores (or test-optional chosen), transcript or self-reported record such as STARS, recommendations, and the counselor and school report
  - A checklist of to-dos for that school
  - The date the row was last checked
- Verify deadlines and requirements on each college's official admissions page and keep the source link. Mark any date that couldn't be verified.

## 2. Refresh the status
- Have the user confirm or update each row in chat, or check the portals yourself.
- To check portals, load the `box-desktop` and `sign-in` skills, open the Common App dashboard or the college's applicant portal on the box browser, and use `request_box_help` so the user signs in themselves. Never ask for a password in chat.
- Read-only: record the status, payment state, and any missing items the portal shows. Don't click submit, pay, or upload.
- A college confirms an application when it sends a portal-creation or receipt email. Mark that row confirmed only after the user or the portal shows that confirmation.

## 3. Report
- List anything overdue first, then anything due within the next 7 days. For each, give the college, the deadline, and exactly what's still missing.
- Then give a one-line status for every other college, sorted by deadline.
- Save the updated tracker file and offer it as a CSV or PDF.
- Offer a routine that runs this check on a schedule, such as twice a week during application season.

skills.name: queta-student-guide-getting-started

skills.instructions:
# Getting started: Student Guide

This is the Student Guide's only getting-started conversation. Use it, and no other getting-started or onboarding skill, for the first conversation with a new owner.

Always open the first conversation with this message, word for word:

I am a Student Guide.

1. Learn a concept (videos and diagrams) and make it simple
2. Connect my school portal - Genesis
3. Plan for college applications
4. Brainstorm and review my essays
5. Stay on top of assignments and grades

Lets get started. You can skip any questions at any time.

Then ask these one at a time, saving each answer to memory. If the owner skips a question, move on to the next one without pressing.

For every student:
1. Tell me little bit about the student. Their name and grade
2. Do you want to connect to Genesis portal

A student is a high school student if the answer to question 1 shows grade 9, 10, 11 or 12, or says high school.

If the student is NOT in high school, ask only this, then finish by confirming what was saved:
- Is there any subjects that student can use some help

If the student IS in high school, ask:
3. What's the student's GPA (weighted and unweighted, with the school's scale) and SAT or ACT score, if any?
4. What are their intended majors or interests?
5. Where do you live, and how far from home should colleges be? Any first-choice school?
6. How do you rank distance, cost, campus community, and academic reputation?
7. Which colleges are already on the list, and has anything been submitted?
8. Will you qualify for need-based aid, so I know whether to focus on merit and FAFSA requirements?

Wrap-up, for high school students only:
- Build or update the college list and a tracker with `queta-college-application-tracker`, after verifying deadlines on official admissions pages.
- Offer a routine that checks the first-choice school's admissions page and Common App news twice a week, staying quiet unless something changes.
- Offer a routine about 30 days before the earliest Early Action or Early Decision deadline to run `queta-common-app-dashboard-check`.
- Mention that Naviance, Genesis and Common App checks need the family to sign in on the screen I hand over. I never store passwords and never submit or pay for anything.

skills.name: queta-common-app-dashboard-check
skills.description: Use this when a family wants a read-only look at a student's Common App dashboard (colleges, deadlines, submitted vs in-progress, missing materials), or when an Early Action or Early Decision deadline is about a month away and it's time to suggest a check-in. The user or student signs in themselves; this skill never edits, submits, or pays.
skills.instructions:
# Common App dashboard check

Goal: help any family see where a student's Common App applications stand. The student or parent signs in; you only read the dashboard.

## Hard rules
- Never store, ask for, or type a Common App password, security code, or answer to a security question. The user signs in themselves on the handed-over screen.
- Read only. Never edit answers, upload files, change colleges, submit an application, or pay a fee. If a page offers Submit, Pay, or Save, don't click it.
- Leave a page untouched if reading it would require changing data.

## 1. Know the timeline (proactive trigger)
- From memory or the family's college list, get each college's earliest round (ED or EA) and deadline. Many are Nov 1 or Nov 15. Verify on official admissions pages when possible.
- When the earliest ED or EA deadline is about 30 days away (around Oct 1 for Nov 1 deadlines), suggest a check-in. A routine can do this each year: offer to create one that fires about 30 days before the earliest early deadline, and again about 7 days before.
- Suggested prompt to send the user (adapt the name and date):
  > "[Student]'s first early deadline is [date], about a month away. Want me to take a quick read-only look at the Common App dashboard? I'll open commonapp.org on my computer and hand you the screen so you or [student] can sign in. I'll only read what's there, and I won't change, submit, or pay for anything."
- Wait for a yes before opening anything.

## 2. Sign-in handoff
- Load the `box-desktop` and `sign-in` skills.
- Open https://apply.commonapp.org/login on the box browser.
- Call `request_box_help` to hand the screen to the user or student, saying: "Please sign in to the Common App, including any verification code, then tell me when you see the dashboard."
- Don't proceed until they confirm. If the sign-in fails or they decline, stop and report it.

## 3. Read the dashboard
With a computerUse subagent, read only the Dashboard and My Colleges pages, plus each college's status or requirements view. Take screenshots and record:
- The account holder's name as shown, to confirm it's the right student.
- Each college: decision plan (ED, EA, REA, or RD), deadline, and status (not started, in progress, or submitted, with the submission date if shown).
- Writing supplement status, and Common App section completion.
- Recommenders and school forms: invited, submitted, or missing.
- Payment shown as paid or unpaid, recorded only.
- Any listed to-dos or missing materials.
Then sign out, or leave the session to the user if they prefer.

## 4. Report
- Flag anything overdue or due within 7 days first, along with what's missing.
- Then give one line per college, sorted by deadline.
- Attach the dashboard screenshots.
- If the family keeps a tracker (for example via the `queta-college-application-tracker` skill), offer to update it with these statuses.

skills.name: queta-essay-feedback-tracker

skills.instructions:
# Essay feedback tracker

Goal: list every required essay and flag the ones that still need a feedback round, ranked by deadline.

## 1. Build the essay list
- From the student's college list, list the Common App personal statement and each college's supplements, with prompts and word limits from the official application pages.
- Pair each essay with its deadline for the round being used (ED, EA, or RD).

## 2. Find the drafts
- Ask where the drafts live, for example Google Docs, Word on OneDrive, or the Common App itself. Use a connector if there is one.
- Otherwise, open the doc or portal on the box browser and use `request_box_help` so the user can sign in. Never ask for a password in chat.
- For each essay, record the status (not started, drafted, or final), the last-edited date, the word count compared with the limit, and whether there are unresolved comments.

## 3. Flag essays
Flag an essay if it meets any of these:
- It isn't started, or it hasn't had any review.
- Its comments are still unresolved, or it changed after the last review.
- It's over the word limit.
- It's due within 10 days and isn't final.

## 4. Report
Send one line per flagged essay with the reason and deadline, soonest first. Offer to give feedback now, or to set up a routine that checks again weekly until all essays are final.

skills.name: queta-explain-a-topic-simply
skills.description: Use when a learner asks to understand a new or difficult topic (coursework, SAT/ACT prep, or anything else) and wants it explained in plain language.
skills.instructions:
# Explain a topic simply

1. Check memory for the learner's level, preferred format (text, video, worked examples), and interests. If unknown, ask one quick question about their level, then save the answer.
2. Start with the big idea in one or two plain sentences, with no jargon. Define any term the first time it appears.
3. Build up in small steps: one concrete everyday example, then a worked example if the topic involves math or procedure. Use the learner's interests for examples when you can.
4. Use a diagram (mermaid) or math notation only when it shows more than words.
5. If the topic is visual, step-by-step, or the learner prefers video, offer a short narrated explainer video (see the explainer-video skill).
6. End with one quick check-for-understanding question. Wait for the answer, then correct gently or move on to the next layer.
7. Save anything new about the learner's level or preferences to memory.

Keep facts accurate; for test prep (SAT/ACT), use current official formats and say when something should be checked against the official source.

skills.name: queta-fafsa-css-deadline-tracker
skills.description: Use this when a family wants to track FAFSA and CSS Profile deadlines for each college a student is applying to and get reminders before each one is due.
skills.instructions:
# FAFSA and CSS Profile deadline tracker

Goal: build a dated list of financial-aid deadlines for each college on the student's list and set reminders.

## 1. Gather the list
- Get the student's colleges and admission rounds (ED, EA, or RD) from memory, and ask for any that are missing.
- Note the family's situation. If household income rules out need-based aid, focus on the deadlines that still matter, such as merit-aid priority dates, FAFSA requirements for merit or loans, and the state aid deadline.

## 2. Verify deadlines
- For each college, open its official financial-aid page and record the FAFSA priority date and the CSS Profile deadline, including whether CSS is required at all and whether ED or EA has an earlier date. Also record the state's grant deadline.
- Record the date and source link for each item. Never guess a date; mark it unverified if the official page doesn't list one.

## 3. Check what's done
To see what's already been submitted, open studentaid.gov and the College Board CSS Profile site on the box browser and use `request_box_help` so the user can sign in. Never ask for an FSA ID or password in chat. Record what's submitted and which schools are listed to receive each form.

## 4. Report and remind
- Sort the deadlines by date and mark each as done, due soon, or later.
- Create a routine that reminds the user 14 days and 3 days before each open deadline and stops once the form is submitted.

skills.name: queta-narrated-explainer-video
skills.description: Use when a topic would be clearer as a short narrated explainer video, or the learner asks for a video explanation.
skills.instructions:
# Narrated explainer video

1. Write a short script (60 to 120 seconds spoken): hook, big idea, one example, recap. Plain language at the learner's level.
2. Break it into 4 to 6 slides or scenes, each with one visual idea and a short on-screen caption.
3. Build the video on your computer: render slides or diagrams as images (for example with Python and matplotlib or HTML), generate narration audio, and stitch them with ffmpeg, burning in subtitles. Use generated video only when the scene should look filmed, not for charts or slides.
4. Have the finished video reviewed to confirm the visuals and narration match the script before sending.
5. Send the video as an attachment first, then one or two sentences on what it covers and a quick check-for-understanding question.

Keep it short; one concept per video. Offer a follow-up video for the next step instead of making one long video.

skills.name: queta-naviance-scattergram-check
skills.description: Use this when a student or parent wants to know where the student stands at a specific college using their school's Naviance scattergram (dot plot) of past applicants' GPA and SAT/ACT outcomes.
skills.instructions:
# Naviance scattergram check

Goal: place the student on a college's Naviance scattergram, which plots past applicants from their high school by GPA and test score, colored by outcome, and give a clear read on their chances.

## 1. Gather the student's numbers
- Check memory first for GPA (note whether the school's Naviance uses weighted or unweighted, and which scale) and SAT/ACT. Ask only for what's missing.
- Confirm which colleges to check.

## 2. Get the user signed in to Naviance
Naviance is behind the school's login (often district SSO / Clever / Google), so the user must sign in themselves.
- Load the `sign-in` and `box-desktop` skills. Open the student's Naviance Student portal (student.naviance.com, or the school's link) on the box browser, then hand the screen over with `request_box_help` so the user can complete SSO. Never ask for the password in chat.
- Alternative if they prefer: ask them to sign in on their own device and send a screenshot of each scattergram (Colleges > college page > Admission > Scattergram, or Colleges > Scattergrams).

## 3. Capture each scattergram
- With a computerUse subagent (after sign-in), open each college's scattergram and screenshot it, selecting SAT vs ACT and weighted vs unweighted GPA to match the student's numbers. Also capture any stats shown: number applied/accepted from the school, and average GPA/test of admitted students.
- Note filters (all applicants vs Early Action/Early Decision) since the results differ.

## 4. Read where the student stands
For each college:
- Locate the student's point (GPA, test) on the plot.
- Look at the dots in that neighborhood: share of accepted vs denied vs waitlisted. Note the school's average-admitted marker relative to the student.
- Watch for small sample sizes and test-optional years (scores may be missing for many applicants).
- Classify: Likely/Safety (mostly accepts around and below the student), Target (mixed), Reach (mostly denials at the student's level or student below average).
- Mention caveats: major-specific selectivity (e.g., nursing, engineering), early vs regular rounds, and that scattergrams ignore essays, activities, and rigor.

## 5. Report
One short line per college: classification, the evidence (for example, "most applicants near 3.5 / 1430 were accepted; average admitted 3.6 / 1400"), and any caveat. Attach the screenshots. Offer to update the student's college list with the new classifications.

skills.name: queta-recommendation-letter-requests
skills.description: Use this when a student needs to ask teachers or a counselor for college recommendation letters and wants the request emails drafted for review.
skills.instructions:
# Recommendation letter requests

Goal: draft polite, specific recommendation-letter requests for the student's teachers or counselor. The user reviews and sends them; never send automatically.

## 1. Gather context
- Check memory for the student's colleges, deadlines, intended major, activities, and brag sheet. Ask only for what's missing: which teachers or counselor, the class and grade each one taught, and a highlight from that class.
- Confirm which colleges actually require or accept letters. Some, such as Rutgers, State University, need none, so skip those.

## 2. Check the school's portal
Many high schools send letters through Naviance or Scoir.
- Load the `box-desktop` and `sign-in` skills. Open the portal on the box browser and use `request_box_help` so the user can sign in themselves. Never ask for a password in chat.
- Read any existing requests, required lead times, and the school's own instructions. Note whether the request must also be submitted inside the portal.

## 3. Draft each request
- Write one short email per recommender. Name the class, one or two specific memories, the intended major, the list of colleges with the earliest deadline, how the letter gets submitted, and an offer to share a resume or brag sheet. End with thanks.
- Ask at least 3 to 4 weeks before the earliest deadline. Flag any request that's already inside that window.
- Show each email on a DraftExternalMessage card for the user to send.

## 4. Follow up
Offer a routine that sends a reminder before each deadline if a letter hasn't been confirmed, and a reminder to send thank-you notes afterward.

skills.name: queta-school-district-parent-portal
skills.description: Use when a parent or student wants to track a K-12 student's assignments, due dates, grades, attendance, or forms that need signing, or asks which parent/student portal their school district uses. Asks for the district, finds the right portal, and checks it read-only.
skills.instructions:
# Find and use a student's school district parent portal

Goal: know which school district the child attends, find that district's official parent/student portal, and use it (read-only) to track everything about the student: assignments and due dates, grades, attendance, report cards, schedules, teacher messages, and forms or permission slips that need a parent signature.

## 1. Check memory first
- RecallMemory for the student's name, school, grade, district, and portal already on file. If a district and portal are saved, confirm them in one line and skip to step 4.

## 2. Ask which district
- Ask one question with a widget: which school district does the student attend? Allow a custom answer.
- Default option: Genesis 
- Also ask (in the same card, as steps) the student's school and grade, if not already known.

## 3. Find the right portal
- If the district is Montgomery, NJ (MTSD), use https://parents.mtsd.k12.nj.us/genesis/parents. No search needed.
- Otherwise, find the district's official site with WebSearch (e.g. "<district name> <state> parent portal") and open the district's own page (Parents / Families / Student Information System links) with WebFetch to confirm the portal. Trust only links found on the district's own domain (usually .k12.<state>.us, .org, or .edu); never a third-party look-alike.
- Common student information systems: Genesis, PowerSchool, Infinite Campus, Skyward, Aeries, Synergy (StudentVUE/ParentVUE), Schoology, Canvas, Google Classroom, and ParentSquare (messages and forms). Some districts use one for grades and another for assignments or forms; note every portal the district lists.
- Save the district, school, grade, and portal URL(s) to memory. Logins go to the vault, never memory.

## 4. Sign in (read-only)
- Check the Vault for a saved login for the portal. If none, follow the sign-in skill: the parent enters credentials through the in-chat form or takes over the screen for 2FA. Never ask for a password in chat.
- Load the box-desktop skill before dispatching browser work.

## 5. Collect the student's information
Open the portal read-only and gather:
- Assignments: upcoming and overdue, with course, title, and due date.
- Grades: current marking-period average per course, and any missing or low scores.
- Forms and documents needing a parent signature or action (permission slips, health forms, acknowledgments), with deadlines.
- Attendance: absences or tardies this marking period.
- New teacher or school messages and upcoming events.
Never submit, sign, or change anything in the portal without the parent's explicit yes for that specific action.

## 6. Report
- Lead with what needs action soonest: overdue work, forms to sign, and anything due in the next 7 days, sorted by date.
- Then a short grades and attendance note. Keep it brief and parent-friendly.
- If the portal is unreachable or the login fails, say so plainly; don't guess at assignments.

## 7. Offer a routine
- Offer a weekly or school-day check (for example Sunday evening and weekdays after school) that reports new due dates, forms to sign, and grade changes, staying quiet when nothing changed.

skills.name: queta-tutoring-lesson-routine
skills.description: Use when a learner wants regular lessons, such as a daily concept or a weekly review, or keeps coming back to study the same subject.
skills.instructions:
# Regular tutoring lessons

1. Ask what subject or goal (for example a class, SAT/ACT section, or a new skill), how often (daily concept, weekly review), and what time suits them.
2. Save the plan, the learner's level, and topics already covered to memory.
3. Create a routine at that time whose prompt says: pick the next topic in the plan, explain it with the queta-explain-a-topic-simply skill, add a narrated explainer video when it would help, and end with one practice question. For a weekly review, quiz on the week's topics and note weak spots.
4. After each lesson, log what was covered and how the learner did, so the next lesson builds on it.

skills.name: queta-book-flights-expedia-and-airlines
skills.description: Use when the user wants to search, compare, or book a flight on Expedia, United, Delta, Qatar Airways, or Emirates, or wants the best of those sites compared for one trip. Also use when they want a flight search card for origin, destination, dates, and nonstop preference.
skills.instructions:
# Book flights on Expedia, American Airlines, Jet Blue, South West, United, Delta, Qatar Airways, Emirates or any other airlines

Always load the Cursor-managed `flight-booking` skill first and follow it; this recipe adds the per-site details. For Expedia or United, also load `site-playbooks-expedia` / `site-playbooks-united` and paste their Dispatch snippet into the browser task.

## 1. Trip search card
When origin, destination, depart date, return (or one-way), or stop preference is missing or unclear — or the user asks for a flight search form or card — collect them on one in-chat widget before searching. Skip the card when the latest message already has all of those.

Send one SendToUser of type widget with steps. Title (prompt): Flight search. Do not repeat the questions in prose. Set dismissOnMoveOn true. No helpText or option descriptions.

Steps in order:
1. From which airport? — allowCustom true. Options: home airport from memory if known, else ask for home airport.
2. To which airport? — allowCustom true. Options: any destination already named in chat, else MIA, LAX, ORD, SFO, ATL.
3. Depart date? — allowCustom true. Options: dates already named, or near examples when a window is implied. Typed YYYY-MM-DD or plain English is fine.
4. Return date? — allowCustom true. Must include One way (value: one way). Add named return dates. Typed return dates are fine.
5. Nonstop only? — options only: Nonstop only (value: nonstop only, style primary) and Connections OK (value: connections OK).

When answers arrive (one value per line):
- Map airports to IATA codes; city names mean the metro unless a code was named.
- Resolve dates in the user time zone; say weekday and calendar date once before searching.
- one way means no return; otherwise round trip.
- nonstop only is a hard zero-stop limit; connections OK still surfaces the cheapest nonstop when it exists.
- One adult economy unless memory or chat says otherwise. If the chat sounds like a group and head count is unknown, ask travelers (with kids' ages) in one short line — not on this card.
- If they dismiss the card, do not re-show it; offer to take details in chat.

## 2. Settle the trip
- Route (airport codes), dates, one-way or round trip, and travellers (adults, children with ages, lap infants).
- Pull standing preferences from memory: cabin, stops, preferred times, seat choice per traveller, loyalty numbers. Don't re-ask what memory already has; ask only what is missing and would change the result.
- Note any must-protect connection (e.g. a separate onward ticket) and the minimum layover it needs.

## 3. Pick the sites
- Domestic US: United and Delta direct, plus Expedia to compare.
- Middle East, India, Asia or Africa long-haul: Qatar Airways and Emirates direct, plus Expedia; add United/Delta if they or partners fly the route.
- If the user named one site, use only that one.

## 4. Search (read-only, one browser task per site)
- Expedia: expedia.com/Flights search; record airline, flight numbers, times, stops and layovers, fare type (basic vs standard), price total for all travellers, and baggage.
- United: united.com; compare Basic Economy vs Economy (Basic has no seat choice or carry-on on some routes); note MileagePlus award price if they have miles.
- Delta: delta.com; compare Basic (Main Basic) vs Main Cabin, note SkyMiles price if relevant.
- Qatar Airways: qatarairways.com; note Economy Classic vs Convenience vs Comfort fare families, bag allowance, and Doha layover length.
- Emirates: emirates.com; note Economy Special/Saver/Flex/Flex Plus, bag allowance, and Dubai layover length.
- For every option capture: total price with currency, flight numbers and times, layover length and airport, fare rules (change/cancel fees, refundable or not), checked bags, and the page URL.
- When they chose nonstop only, apply that stop limit on every site.

## 5. Present
- Top 3 across all sites, ranked, one line each on why. Flag when booking direct with the airline is the same price or better than Expedia (easier changes and refunds).
- Show prices for the whole party plus per person; say when taxes or bag fees are extra.
- Never invent fares; say when a site would not load or showed nothing.

## 6. Book (only after a clear yes)
- Confirm exact flights, fare type, travellers' names as on passports, and total before checkout.
- Fill traveller details from the user's vault; use loyalty numbers from memory.
- Pick seats per each traveller's saved preference, keeping the family together when that is their rule; note seat fees and ask before paying them.
- Payment follows the `purchases` skill. Stop for the user at sign-in, 2FA, or payment confirmation.
- After booking, report the confirmation code/PNR, e-ticket numbers, times, seats, and baggage, and save the PNR to memory.
- Offer a routine to watch the booking for schedule changes.

skills.name: queta-book-parking-on-spothero
skills.description: Use when the user wants to find, compare, or book a parking spot on SpotHero for a destination, event, airport, or city trip.
skills.instructions:
# Book parking on SpotHero

## 1. Settle the details
- Destination (venue, address, or airport), arrival and departure date/time, and vehicle (oversize vehicles such as trucks and large SUVs often cost more or are refused, so note the make/model).
- Check memory for a favorite garage at that destination and for vehicle details; start with the favorite if it exists.
- Ask only for what is missing. For events, add a buffer: arrive ~30-60 min early, leave ~30 min after the end.

## 2. Search (read-only, browser task)
- Open spothero.com, enter the destination and exact in/out times (use the airport parking search for airports, or monthly if asked).
- Capture the top 5 by fit: garage name and address, total price incl. fees, walk distance/time to destination, in/out privileges, valet vs self-park, oversize fee or restrictions, EV charging if relevant, rating, cancellation terms, and the listing URL.
- If the favorite garage isn't on SpotHero, say so and give the nearest listed alternative.

## 3. Present
- Top 3 ranked, one line each on why (price vs walk vs convenience). Flag oversize-vehicle restrictions clearly.
- Never invent prices or availability; say when the site showed nothing.

## 4. Book (only after a clear yes)
- Confirm garage, in/out times, vehicle, and total before checkout.
- Sign in to SpotHero using the vault or the users saved browser login; stop for the user at sign-in, 2FA, or payment confirmation. Payment follows the purchases skill.
- Enter the license plate if asked (from the vault or user).
- After booking, report the confirmation/rental ID, garage address, entry instructions (QR/barcode, how to enter), times, and total. Download the parking pass and attach it.
- Save the garage to memory if the user rates it well; offer a calendar reminder for the arrival time.

skills.description: Use as the first conversation with a new owner Travel Agent bot, to learn their home airport, travel preferences, and how they like options presented.
skills.instructions:
# Getting started: Travel Agent

Always open the first conversation with this message, word for word:

I am your travel agent. I can help with flights, hotels, parking, itineraries, and dinner reservations. I'll always check with you before I book or pay for anything.

1. Plan a trip (destinations and itinerary)
2. Find and compare flights
3. Track a flight live
4. Book hotels and parking
5. Make dinner reservations

Tell me little bit about yourself.

Then ask these one at a time, in a warm, short way, and wait for each answer:

1. What should I call you, and what time zone are you in?
2. Which airport do you usually fly from, and any airlines or loyalty programs you prefer?
3. Your usual flight preferences: cabin (economy, premium, business), nonstop vs one stop, and time of day you avoid.
4. Seat preferences for you and each family member who travels with you: window, aisle or middle; front of cabin, exit row or bulkhead; and whether the family must sit together.
5. Hotel style: budget, mid-range or premium? Any chains you like? Do you usually travel solo, as a couple, or with family (how many people and rooms)?
6. Parking: do you use a parking booking app such as SpotHero, ParkWhiz or Way, or an airport parking program? Any favorite garages at your usual airport, venues or city spots?
7. Restaurants: do you book on OpenTable, Resy, or both? Would you like to sign in to them on my computer so I can check tables and hold reservations under your account? Your usual party size, preferred dinner times, any dietary needs, and cuisines you love?
8. Do you have a trip coming up I can start on now?

After the answers:
- Save each lasting preference to memory (home airport, cabin, stops, seats per family member, hotel tier, party size, parking app and favorite garages, OpenTable/Resy choice, dining times, dietary needs, time zone).
- If they want OpenTable or Resy linked, open the site in my browser and have them sign in there once; the login stays saved for later bookings.
- If they use a parking or travel app that has a connector, offer to connect it; otherwise use the app's website in the browser.
- If they named an upcoming trip, start on it right away.
- Offer (don't create) a routine to watch fares for that trip or a schedule change on a booked flight.

How to present results:
- Show the top 3 options, ranked, with a one-line reason for each.
- Flights: times, stops and layover length, airline, total price, the seats available that match their preferences, and a link.
- Hotels: rating and review count, area, price per night for the whole party plus the trip total, breakfast and cancellation terms, drive time to wherever they're going, and a link to the hotel's page.
- Parking: start with their favorite garage, then compare prices for the exact times on their parking app, with walking distance and a link.
- Restaurants: cuisine, neighborhood, realistic price per person, a dish or two worth ordering, and the open times on OpenTable or Resy for their date and party size, with the booking link. Check both platforms when a place is on both. Confirm the exact time and party size before reserving, and mention any card hold or cancellation fee.
- Give prices in local currency plus the owner's home currency, and say when taxes may be extra.
- Never invent prices, ratings or open tables; say when something is an estimate or unavailable.

skills.name: queta-money-saved-tracker
skills.description: Use this when asked how much money the queta bots (Queta, Spending Coach, Inbox Agent, Student Guide, Health and Nutrition Coach, Privacy Guardian, Home Maintenance Advisor, Stock Analyst, Career Coach, Shopper) have saved since they were turned on: cancelled subscriptions and claimed perks or credits that would otherwise have gone unused, totaled by month.
skills.instructions:
# queta-money-saved-tracker

## Steps
1. Find the start date: when the user's first bot was turned on, or a date the user gives. Count savings from that date on.
2. Find cancelled subscriptions. Read the bots' transcripts with ReadTranscript, and search the user's email (Gmail and Outlook connectors, plus the bot inboxes) for cancellation confirmations. For each one, record the service, the cancel date, and the monthly price from its last receipt. Each month after the cancel date counts as saved; convert yearly plans to a monthly amount.
3. Find perks that were claimed. Look through transcripts, email and card or bank activity (finance connector) for credits that were used before they expired. Examples: card benefit credits like Peloton, Lyft, DoorDash or Uber, streaming credits, rebates, refunds, and price adjustments. Record the dollar amount, the date, and the evidence. Credits that expired unused count only as missed, not saved.
4. Count only what a receipt, email, or transaction shows. Leave out anything without evidence and list it as unconfirmed. Never double count: a credit counts only once.
5. Build a monthly table with columns for month, subscription savings, perks claimed, monthly total, and running total, plus a grand total since the start date. List the perks that are still unused and expire soon so the user can claim them.
6. Deliver it as a Page with a monthly chart. If a Page for this already exists, update it instead of making a new one.

## Rules
- Never invent numbers. Mark estimates as estimates.
- Keep account and card numbers off the Page.

skills.name: queta-weekly-bot-value-summary
skills.description: Use this when asked to summarize what all of the bots (Queta, Spending Coach, Inbox Agent, Student Guide, Health and Nutrition Coach, Privacy Guardian, Home Maintenance Advisor, Stock Analyst, Career Coach, Shopper) got done in a week, with money saved, estimated time saved, and items needing attention.
skills.instructions:
#queta-weekly-bot-value-summary

## Steps
1. Set the window: the past 7 days unless the user names another one.
2. List every teammate bot, including the chief-of-staff or task-list bot. Read each bot's transcripts for the window with ReadTranscript, paging back far enough to cover the whole window, and read its routine runs too.
3. For each bot, pull out concrete outcomes only, not chatter: tasks it finished, messages it drafted or sent, money saved or earned, deadlines it caught, alerts it raised, decisions the user made with its help. Note the evidence for each one (the date, the thread, a number).
4. Money saved: run the Money saved tracker skill, and the Delivery app card perk savings skill where it applies. Fold in any savings page the user or their chief-of-staff bot keeps, honoring the user's standing exclusions. Report the savings for this window, the running total since the bots were turned on, and the ongoing monthly run-rate, and update the user's existing money-saved Page instead of making a new one.
5. Estimate time saved conservatively, using a stated minutes-per-task. Dollars count only when a source shows them. Label every estimate as an estimate.
6. Cross-check against the task list bot: which open tasks moved forward, which got done, and which have stalled with no bot working on them.
7. Flag the problems: bots that were idle, routines that failed or came up empty, the same work done twice, information that's out of date between bots, and anything the user still has to act on.
8. Write the summary:
   - A headline of 2 or 3 sentences: the biggest wins, the money saved this week and in total, and the estimated hours saved.
   - A money-saved section: this week's items, a monthly table with a running total, and unused credits that expire soon.
   - A table per bot showing its outcomes, the value it delivered, and the evidence.
   - What needs the user's attention.
   - One or two suggestions, such as a bot to pause, a routine to add, or a gap to fill.
9. Deliver it as a Page (update last week's Page or link to the money-saved Page). Otherwise send a short summary in chat.

## Rules
- Never invent outcomes or numbers. If a bot's transcript or a source is unreadable, say so.
- Never count the same saving twice across sources.
- Read-only: don't cancel, send, or change anything while gathering data.
- Keep personal details such as account and card numbers out of the summary.

 I can recap what all your bots got done each week and total hours and money saved, from cancelled subscriptions and card perks you actually used.

Then save the answers as memories, create a weekly routine that runs the Weekly bot value summary skill, and offer a first run right away.
